entry: Epic poem in blank verse by English poet [[John Milton]]. It retells the biblical story of the fall of man: the temptation of [[Adam and Eve]] by the fallen angel [[Satan]] and their expulsion from the [[Garden of Eden]]. The first version, published in 1667, had ten books. A second edition in 1674 reorganized it into twelve books, in the manner of Virgil's *Aeneid*, with minor revisions. Milton composed the poem by dictation after going blind in 1652. Adam and Eve are presented as having a romantic and sexual relationship before sin. After eating the fruit, they experience lust for the first time, then guilt and shame. Milton's stated purpose is to "justify the ways of God to men." It is considered Milton's masterpiece.

Logically self-contradictory statement, or one that runs contrary to expectations. Despite apparently valid reasoning from true premises, a paradox leads to a seemingly contradictory or unacceptable conclusion. In [[Logic|logic]], many paradoxes are invalid arguments yet valuable for promoting [[Critical thinking]], while others have exposed flawed definitions and forced re-examination of logical axioms. [[Russell's paradox]], which asks whether a "list of all lists that do not contain themselves" includes itself, showed that attempts to found [[Set theory]] on properties were flawed. Examples outside logic include the [[Ship of Theseus]], which asks whether a ship with every wooden part replaced remains the same ship. In many drawings, [[M. C. Escher]] used perspective paradoxes, with walls that are floors from other viewpoints. Self-reference, contradiction and infinite regress are core elements of many paradoxes.

Soft colorless solid derived from [[Petroleum|petroleum]], coal or oil shale. It consists of hydrocarbon molecules with 20 to 40 carbon atoms and is insoluble in water. Carl Reichenbach first made it in Germany in 1830. It burned more cleanly and cheaply than tallow candles, and it is used in [[Candle|candles]], lubrication, electrical insulation and crayons. In chemistry, paraffin is a synonym for [[Alkane|alkane]]. The name comes from Latin *parum* ("very little") and *affinis* ("lacking affinity"), referring to its unreactive nature.

Landlocked republic in central [[South America]]. Its capital and largest city is [[Asunción]]. Paraguay borders [[Bolivia]], [[Brazil]] and [[Argentina]], and reaches the Atlantic Ocean by the Paraná–Paraguay Waterway. Spanish conquistadors arrived in 1524, and Asunción was founded in 1537. Jesuit missions in the 17th century converted Indigenous peoples to Christianity. Paraguay dates its independence from Spain to 1811. The Triple Alliance War (1864–1870) cost it much of its population and around 25–33% of its territory, and the Chaco War with Bolivia (1932–1935) followed. [[Alfredo Stroessner]] ruled for 35 years until a military coup in 1989 began the current democratic era. The economy relies on beef and soybean exports, manufacturing and construction. Paraguay is one of the world's leading exporters of hydroelectricity, notably from the [[Itaipu Dam]] on the Paraná River. Most Paraguayans are mestizo, and more than 90% speak Guarani alongside Spanish.

Conflict in [[South America]], fought from 1864 to 1870 between [[Paraguay]] and the Triple Alliance of Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay. Also called the War of the Triple Alliance, it was the deadliest interstate war in Latin American history. It began in late 1864 from a conflict between Paraguay and Brazil arising from the Uruguayan War, and Argentina and Uruguay joined in 1865. After Paraguay lost conventional battles, it waged a guerrilla resistance for 14 months, which further destroyed its army and civilians, many of whom died from battle, hunger and disease. President Francisco Solano López was killed by Brazilian forces at the Battle of Cerro Corá on March 1, 1870. Paraguay ceded disputed territory to Argentina and Brazil, and Argentine and Brazilian troops occupied the country until 1876. Estimates of Paraguayan deaths range from 300,000 to 400,000, but casualty figures remain disputed.

Apparent displacement of an object viewed from two different lines of sight. The displacement is measured by the angle between those sight lines, and nearby objects show a larger parallax than distant ones, so parallax can be used to find distances. In astronomy, stellar parallax, observed when Earth is on opposite sides of the [[Sun]] in its orbit, forms the lowest rung of the [[Cosmic distance ladder|cosmic distance ladder]]. German astronomer Friedrich Bessel measured the parallax of 61 Cygni as 0.314 arcseconds in 1838. Parallax also affects optical instruments such as [[Binoculars]] and [[Microscope|microscopes]]. Many animals, including humans, use it for depth perception through stereopsis, in which the brain combines the slightly different views from the two eyes. Parallax scrolling creates an illusion of depth in some 2D video games.

Computation in which many calculations or processes are carried out simultaneously. Large problems are divided into smaller ones that are solved at the same time, using bit-level, instruction-level, data or task parallelism. Parallelism has long been used in high-performance computing. Physical limits on processor frequency scaling, along with concern over power consumption and heat, have made parallelism the dominant paradigm in [[Computer architecture]], chiefly as multi-core processors. In [[Computer science]], parallelism differs from concurrency: parallel programs use several CPU cores at once, while concurrency lets a single core switch between tasks. Clusters and [[Supercomputer|supercomputers]] use multiple computers on one task, and [[Graphics processing unit|GPUs]] accelerate specialized work. Explicitly parallel programs are harder to write, because concurrency introduces bugs such as race conditions. Amdahl's law sets an upper bound on speed-up, limited by the fraction of a program that can be parallelized.

Periodic international multisport event for athletes with a range of [[Disability|disabilities]]. Winter and Summer Paralympic Games have been held shortly after the corresponding [[Olympic Games]] since the 1988 Summer Olympics in [[Seoul]], South Korea, and they are governed by the International Paralympic Committee (IPC). The Paralympics began in 1948 as a small gathering of British veterans of [[World War II]]. The 1960 Games in [[Rome]] drew 400 athletes from 23 countries. The 2020 Summer Paralympics featured 4,520 athletes from 163 National Paralympic Committees. Competitors are grouped into classes by eligible impairment type, of which there are ten, including impaired muscle power, limb deficiency, [[Ataxia]], vision impairment and intellectual impairment.

Indian-born American Hindu monk, yogi and guru. He founded the Self-Realization Fellowship (SRF) to teach [[Yoga|Kriya Yoga]] and [[Meditation|meditation]] in the West. Born Mukunda Lal Ghosh, he trained under the guru Swami Sri Yukteswar Giri and was sent to spread yogic teachings to the West. He moved to the United States in 1920 with the aim of uniting Eastern and Western religions, and settled in [[Los Angeles]] in 1925. Yoga experts consider him the "Father of Yoga in the West." President [[Calvin Coolidge]] hosted him at the White House in 1927, the first prominent Indian to be so hosted. His *Autobiography of a Yogi* (1946) has sold over four million copies, and [[Steve Jobs]] ordered 500 copies of it for guests at his memorial. By 1952 SRF had over 100 centers in India and the United States.

Genus of single-celled [[Ciliate|ciliates]] found in freshwater, brackish and marine habitats. Paramecia are covered with thousands of short, hair-like cilia that beat in rows to propel the cell and sweep food into an oral groove. They typically measure 50 to 350 μm long, and they often abound in stagnant ponds. A large macronucleus controls metabolism and gene expression, while smaller micronuclei are involved in reproduction. Most reproduction is asexual, by transverse binary fission. Sexual reproduction occurs through conjugation, in which compatible mating types exchange genetic material. A contractile vacuole expels excess water in freshwater habitats. Because they are easy to culture, *P. aurelia* and *P. caudatum* are widely used as [[Model organism|model organisms]], and they have been called the "lab rats" of the phylum Ciliophora. *P. bursaria* hosts symbiotic green algae.

Mathematical expression of quantities, such as the coordinates of a point, as functions of one or more parameters. With one parameter, the equations often trace the path of a moving point, forming a [[Curve|parametric curve]]; the parameter is often time, as in [[Kinematics]]. The [[Unit circle]] can be written as x = cos t and y = sin t. Parameterizations are not unique, so one curve can have many parametric representations. Two parameters describe a surface, and more parameters describe higher-dimensional [[Manifold|manifolds]]. A parameter can often be eliminated to recover a Cartesian equation: x = t² and y = t give y² = x, a [[Parabola]].

American rock band formed in Franklin, Tennessee, in 2004, known for pop-punk, [[Alternative rock|alternative rock]] and [[Emo|emo]] influences. Its lineup since 2017 includes vocalist Hayley Williams, guitarist Taylor York and drummer Zac Farro. The second album, *Riot!* (2007), became a mainstream success with the singles "Misery Business" and "That's What You Get." The self-titled 2013 album was the band's first number-one on the Billboard 200. Its single "Ain't It Fun" won a [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]] for Best Rock Song, and *This Is Why* (2023) won the Grammy for Best Rock Album.

American film studio, founded May 8, 1912. It is the second-oldest U.S. studio after [[Universal Pictures]], and one of the Big Four studios along with [[Warner Bros. Pictures]]. Its most commercially successful franchises include *Star Trek*, *Indiana Jones*, *Top Gun*, *Mission: Impossible* and *Transformers*. Its library includes *The Godfather*, *Grease*, *Forrest Gump*, *Titanic* and *Saving Private Ryan*. In 2014 it became the first major Hollywood studio to distribute all its films in digital form only.

River in south-central [[South America]], second in length only to the [[Amazon River]]. It runs about 4,880 km through Brazil, Paraguay and Argentina. The Paraná merges with the Paraguay River and then, downstream, with the [[Uruguay River]] to form the [[Río de la Plata]], which empties into the [[Atlantic Ocean]]. The Venetian explorer Sebastian Cabot was the first European to travel up the river, in 1526, while working for Spain. Its basin supports fisheries and wetlands, and the river carries grain exports. Dams, including the [[Itaipu Dam]] on the Brazil–Paraguay border, generate hydroelectricity. A drought in 2021 brought the river to a 77-year low.

[[Personality disorder]] characterized by pervasive, long-standing suspiciousness and generalized mistrust of others, without adequate basis. Its traits must begin by early adulthood and not occur only during [[Schizophrenia]], bipolar disorder or depressive disorder with psychotic features. Unlike psychotic disorders, it involves no [[Delusion|delusions]] or [[Hallucination|hallucinations]]. Prevalence in the general population is estimated at 0.5% to 4.4%. Its causes are unclear, though adverse childhood experiences are a known risk factor. Treatment is mainly long-term psychotherapy, such as cognitive-behavioral therapy. No medication is approved specifically for it, though drugs may ease co-occurring anxiety or depression.

Purported phenomena outside normal scientific understanding. Such beliefs include extrasensory perception (ESP), such as telepathy, and [[Pseudoscience|pseudosciences]] such as [[Ghost|ghost]] hunting, cryptozoology and ufology. Unlike scientific hypotheses, which rest on empirical observation and experiment under the [[Scientific method]], paranormal claims rest on anecdote, testimony and suspicion. Standard scientific models explain such experiences as misinterpretations or anomalous variations of natural phenomena. Systematic study began in the late 19th century; the Society for Psychical Research was founded in London in 1882. Laboratory experiments on ESP began in 1930 at Duke University under J.B. Rhine. A 2025 U.S. survey found that 39% of respondents believed in ghosts. [[Skepticism|Skeptics]] attribute such beliefs to psychological mechanisms such as sleep paralysis, confirmation bias and perceptual illusions.

Contested genus of extinct hominins, sometimes treated as synonymous with [[Australopithecus]]. Three species are widely accepted: *P. aethiopicus*, *P. robustus* and *P. boisei*. They lived from about 2.9 to at least 1.2 million years ago, from the end of the [[Pliocene]] into the Middle Pleistocene. Their robust skulls had prominent sagittal crests, which suggest strong chewing muscles, and broad teeth for grinding. Their bodies were small: males of *P. robustus* were estimated at 40 kg and 132 cm, and males of *P. boisei* at 50 kg and 137 cm. *P. robustus* was probably an omnivore, while *P. boisei* was likely herbivorous. They are associated with bone tools and lived alongside early human species such as *Homo habilis* and *H. erectus*. Large carnivores of the time, including crocodiles, leopards and hyenas, preyed on them.

Intense, persistent sexual interest, arousal or attraction to anything not typically considered sexual within a given culture. Also called a sexual fetish or kink. Paraphilias are contrasted with normophilic interests that conform to [[Social norm|social norms]], though the distinction is controversial. The DSM-5 separates paraphilias from paraphilic disorders, which involve distress, impairment or nonconsenting people, and names eight paraphilic disorders. Although once thought rare, paraphilic interests are relatively common. Anil Aggrawal has listed as many as 549 types. Treatment of disorders typically involves cognitive-behavioral therapy or drugs that reduce urges.

2019 South Korean black comedy thriller directed by Bong Joon Ho. A poor family infiltrates the household of a wealthy family. It premiered at the [[Cannes Film Festival]] in May 2019, where it won the Palme d'Or, the first Korean film to do so. At the 92nd [[Academy Awards]] it won Best Picture, the first non-English-language film to do so, and also Best Director, Best Original Screenplay and Best International Feature Film. In 2025 [[The New York Times]] ranked it the best movie of the 21st century so far, in a poll of readers, actors and directors.

Close interaction between species in which a parasite, living on or in a host, harms it. Parasites range from single-celled protozoans, such as the agents of [[Malaria]] and sleeping sickness, to animals such as hookworms, lice and vampire bats, and plants such as mistletoe. Unlike [[Predation|predators]], parasites are usually much smaller than their hosts and usually do not kill them, and they often live in or on a host for an extended period. An endoparasite lives inside its host, and an ectoparasite lives on its surface. Parasitism shades into predation through parasitoidism, and through evolution into mutualism. Human knowledge of parasites dates to ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome, and [[Antonie van Leeuwenhoek]] observed *Giardia lamblia* in 1681. In fiction, Bram Stoker's *Dracula* (1897) features a blood-drinking parasite.

Writing material made from the prepared, untanned skins of animals, primarily sheep, calves and goats. It was used as a writing medium in West Asia and Europe for more than two millennia. By 400 AD, many works intended for preservation had been transferred from [[Papyrus]] to parchment. According to ancient sources, it was developed at Pergamum in the second century BC as an alternative after an export embargo from Egypt. Vellum is a finer parchment made from calfskin. Hides are soaked in water and lime, scraped, stretched on a frame and smoothed with [[Pumice]]. One hide yields only a few sheets; a 229-folio book required about 115 skins. Parchment dominated early [[Middle Ages|medieval]] Northwestern Europe, especially for illuminated manuscripts and legal documents, until cheaper [[Paper|paper]] spread from the 12th century. It remains sensitive to humidity and water.

Progenitor of an offspring or, in humans, a caregiver or legal guardian such as an adoptive parent or stepparent. Parents are first-degree relatives who share 50% of their genes with their children. A female can become a parent through [[Surrogacy]], and orphans may be raised by [[Grandparent|grandparents]] or other relatives. The most common types of parents are mothers, fathers, stepparents and grandparents. In humans, a mother typically supplies the egg and gestates the [[Fetus|fetus]], while a father provides sperm for fertilization. Parental care, including provisioning, protection and education, improves offspring survival. The degree of parental involvement considered acceptable varies by culture; too little may be called neglect, and too much may be called overprotective.

Empirical rule of thumb: roughly 80% of effects from 20% of causes. Also called the 80:20 rule or the law of the vital few, it is named after [[Vilfredo Pareto]], an Italian economist who observed that about 80% of land in the [[Kingdom of Italy]] was owned by 20% of the population. In 1941 management consultant Joseph M. Juran developed the concept for quality control. The rule is associated with the power-law distribution called the Pareto distribution. Ratios vary, and critics note that the principle is a heuristic that risks oversimplification.

Revolutionary government in [[Paris]] that held power from March 18 to May 28, 1871. It arose after the French defeat in the [[Franco-Prussian War]], when National Guard soldiers seized the city and refused to accept the authority of the Third Republic. The Commune's policies included the separation of church and state, the remission of rents, the abolition of child labor and the closing of Catholic churches and schools. Socialist, feminist and anarchist currents all played roles. National forces under [[Adolphe Thiers]] crushed it in a "bloody week" beginning May 21, 1871, killing an estimated 10,000 to 15,000 Communards. The Commune had executed about one hundred hostages, including Archbishop Georges Darboy. Of about 15,000 people tried, 13,500 were convicted, and 1,169 were sentenced to deportation, mostly to [[New Caledonia]]. [[Karl Marx]] and [[Friedrich Engels]] described the Commune as the first example of the dictatorship of the proletariat.

American media personality and businesswoman, great-granddaughter of Hilton Hotels founder Conrad Hilton. She drew tabloid attention for her presence in [[New York City]]'s social scene in the late 1990s and was proclaimed "New York's leading It Girl" in 2001. The reality series *The Simple Life* (2003–2007), co-starring Nicole Richie, made her a global figure. Her career spans acting, modeling, singing, writing and podcasting, and her perfume line has brought in over US$2.5 billion in revenue, as of 2020. Critics describe her as a celebutante, and [[Forbes]] ranked her the most "overexposed" celebrity in 2006 and 2008.
